name: Commitizen (cz-cli)
summary: A Node.js command, `git cz`, that replaces `git commit` with a set of prompts and assembles your answers into a message in the project’s chosen format, usually Conventional Commits.
intro: Instead of typing a free-form message, you run `git cz` (or `npx cz`) and answer questions: what type of change, which scope, a short subject, a longer body, which issues it closes. Commitizen itself only provides the command and the prompt plumbing. The questions and the format come from an adapter, an npm module that a repository names in `package.json` under `config.commitizen.path` or in a `.czrc` file. The adapter gets an Inquirer.js instance to ask its questions and hands back a string, which Commitizen passes to `git commit` together with any other `git commit` flags you gave.

The usual adapter is cz-conventional-changelog, which writes messages in the Angular convention that became Conventional Commits (`feat(search): add filter by price range`) and caps the header line at 100 characters by default. Others add Jira ticket ids, emoji or fully custom questions. `commitizen init cz-conventional-changelog --save-dev --save-exact` installs an adapter and writes the config in one step. In a repository with no config, `git cz` behaves like plain `git commit`.

Commitizen is meant to run beside commit hooks, not replace them: it helps a contributor write a valid message up front, while a hook or CI check such as commitlint rejects invalid ones afterward. It can also run from Git’s `prepare-commit-msg` hook (`cz --hook`), so a plain `git commit` opens the prompts. Not to be confused with the Python project of the same name (commitizen-tools/commitizen), a separate tool that also provides a `cz` command and adds version bumping and changelog generation.
strengths: Contributors don’t have to read CONTRIBUTING.md to learn the message format: the prompts ask for each required field
Adapters are plain npm packages, so many repositories can share one convention, and teams can write their own
Pairs with tools that read the same format, such as commitlint (which ships a Commitizen adapter) and conventional-changelog, because the messages come out in the expected shape
`cz --retry` replays the last attempted message after a failing pre-commit hook, so you don’t re-answer every prompt
limits: It only shapes messages from people who use it; anyone running plain `git commit` bypasses it, so enforcement still needs a commit-msg hook or a CI check
Node.js only: the README still lists testing against Node.js 12, 14 and 16, and you need npm to install it and its adapter
Development has slowed: the last feature release was 4.3.0 (January 2023, adding pnpm to `init`); 4.3.1 (September 2024) and 4.3.2 (June 2026) fixed bugs and dependencies
Running it from a Git hook needs `exec < /dev/tty` because hooks aren’t interactive, and with husky an npm script named `commit` makes `precommit` scripts run twice

snippet.title: Make a repository “Commitizen friendly” and commit through the prompts
source: npx cz            # prompts for type, scope, subject, body and issues
# -> feat(search): add filter by price range
npx cz --retry    # reuse the last answers after a failed pre-commit hook

story: Projects with a structured commit format, such as AngularJS, whose commit guidelines the conventional-changelog tool was built around, documented the rules in a CONTRIBUTING file and relied on Git hooks to reject messages that broke them. Contributors had to dig the format out of the docs, or found out about it when a hook rejected their commit.

Jim Cummins published Commitizen to npm in April 2015 with a one-line description: “Git commit, but play nice with conventions.” Its first README set out the idea that still defines it: prompt contributors for the required fields at commit time instead of rejecting their commits later, and let each project pick a convention through an adapter, starting with cz-conventional-changelog for the Angular format. It described itself as a project that helps contributors be good open-source citizens.

Its README now points to conventional-changelog and commitlint as related projects, and commitlint ships its own Commitizen adapter. The configuration moved from a `.cz.json` file to `package.json` and `.czrc`, version 4.0.0 (July 2019) dropped Node.js 6 and 8, and 4.2.0 (August 2020) added the short `cz` binary name. Since 4.3.0 in January 2023 the project has mostly received maintenance releases.

choices.choice: Prompt at commit time instead of rejecting afterward
choices.why: Waiting for a hook to reject a message, or digging through CONTRIBUTING.md to find the format, made contributing harder. Asking for each field up front gives instant feedback.

choices.choice: Put the convention in a pluggable adapter
choices.why: Every project and build process has different requirements, so Commitizen keeps only the command and delegates the questions and format to npm modules that many projects can share.

choices.choice: Work beside commit hooks, not instead of them
choices.why: The authors treat committing as a declaration of intent to contribute; the maintainer decides the rules, and hooks remain useful to enforce them for people who don’t use the prompts.
